front: In process instrumentation, what is a transmitter?
back: A device that produces an output signal for its measurement, for example a 4–20 mA electrical current.
excerpt: A transmitter is a device that produces an output signal

front: How do you calculate the percentage of range that a 4–20 mA loop current I represents?
back: Percent of range = (I − 4 mA) / 16 mA × 100 %. So 4 mA gives 0 % and 20 mA gives 100 %.
excerpt: with the two values of 4 and 20 mA representing 0–100% of the range of measurement or control
mnemonic: Take off the live zero (4), divide by the span (16): 12 mA is halfway, 50 %.

front: Why does the 4–20 mA signal range start at 4 mA rather than 0 mA?
back: The 'live zero' keeps current flowing so the loop can still power the field device when the measured value is at its minimum.
excerpt: allows powering of the device even with no process signal output from the field transmitter
mnemonic: Live zero: zero signal, but the wire is still alive with 4 mA to feed the device.

front: Why does a 4–20 mA receiver treat a current below 3.8 mA as a fault, not a low reading?
back: A genuine minimum reading (0%) still gives 4 mA, so a current below the signal range is taken to indicate a fault.
excerpt: It is self-monitoring; currents less than 3.8 mA or more than 20.5 mA are taken to indicate a fault.

front: Why does voltage drop along a long cable not falsify a current-loop signal?
back: The current is the same at every point of the loop, so the receiver measures exactly the current the transmitter set.
excerpt: Basic DC circuit theory shows that the current is the same all along the line.

back: An electrically operated switch: a control signal on its input terminals opens or closes contacts that switch a separate circuit.
excerpt: A relay is an electrically operated switch. It has a set of input terminals for one or more control signals, and a set of operating contact terminals.

front: How does energising the coil of an electromechanical relay move its contacts?
back: Current in the coil generates a magnetic field that pulls the iron armature, and the armature moves the contacts to make or break a connection.
excerpt: When an electric current is passed through the coil it generates a magnetic field that activates the armature

front: What does a normally closed (NC) relay contact do when the relay coil is energised?
back: It opens and disconnects its circuit; with the coil unpowered it is closed and the circuit is connected.
excerpt: Normally closed (NC) contacts disconnect the circuit when the relay is activated; the circuit is connected when the relay is inactive.

front: Why is a flyback diode placed across a relay coil that is driven with direct current?
back: Switching the coil off collapses its magnetic field, producing a voltage spike; the diode dissipates that energy and protects semiconductor components.
excerpt: to dissipate the energy from the collapsing magnetic field (back EMF) at deactivation, which would otherwise generate a voltage spike dangerous to semiconductor circuit components

front: How is a solid-state relay built differently from an electromechanical relay?
back: It has no moving parts: a semiconductor switching device, such as a thyristor, switches the load in place of coil-driven contacts.
excerpt: A solid-state relay uses a thyristor, TRIAC or other solid-state switching device, activated by the control signal, to switch the controlled load, instead of a solenoid.

front: How does an optocoupler pass a signal between two circuits without connecting them electrically?
back: A light-emitting diode on one side shines on a phototransistor on the other, so the signal crosses as light and the circuits stay isolated.
excerpt: An optocoupler (a light-emitting diode (LED) coupled with a photo transistor) can be used to isolate control and controlled circuits.

front: Why can a safety circuit trust a monitoring contact on a relay with force-guided contacts?
back: All contacts are mechanically linked, so a normally closed monitoring contact can close only if every normally open contact is open, exposing a stuck contact.
excerpt: it then becomes possible to guarantee that if any NC contact is closed, all NO contacts are open
mnemonic: Force-guided contacts move as one rigid block: one stuck contact freezes them all, so the monitoring contact cannot lie.
